pos: n. (the landgraviate whose prince called the Marburg Colloquy, founded the first Protestant university, and disgraced the cause by his bigamy)
etymology: German Hessen, from the Chatti, the Germanic people of the region named by Tacitus; Latin Hassia.
biblical_def: Hesse is the German principality whose landgrave did the Reformation its greatest political service and its greatest private injury. Philip of Hesse took the Reformation into his lands from 1526, held the Homberg Synod in that year and had a church order drafted by Francois Lambert, founded Marburg in 1527 as the first university established as a Protestant foundation, and was with the Elector of Saxony the chief organiser of the Schmalkaldic League, the defensive alliance that kept the evangelical states in being. He saw further than most that the Lutheran and the Swiss must not divide, and it was he who summoned Luther, Zwingli, Bucer, Oecolampadius and Melanchthon to the Marburg Colloquy of October 1529; they agreed on fourteen articles and parted over the fifteenth, the presence of Christ in the Supper. In 1540 Philip, already married, took a second wife, having extracted from Luther, Melanchthon and Bucer a secret and shameful counsel permitting it as a dispensation; the matter became public, cost him his political standing, and gave the Reformation's enemies their most useful scandal. The dictionary enters Hesse because the record must carry both halves: the colloquy and the league, and the bigamy and the theologians who signed it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a landgrave as a German count having jurisdiction over a territory; a colloquy as a conference or mutual discourse; bigamy as the crime of having two wives at once; and a dispensation as an exemption from a law.
webster_full: LANDGRAVE, n. In Germany, a count or earl; originally an officer with jurisdiction over a territory.
COLLOQUY, n. Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; a conference.
BIGAMY, n. The crime of having two wives at once; the having of a second wife while the first is living.
DISPENSATION, n. The granting of a license, or the license itself, to do what is forbidden by law.
LEAGUE, n. An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense.

Gal 2:11

corruption_summary: Landgraviate whose prince founded Marburg in 1527, called the Marburg Colloquy of 1529 and organised the Schmalkaldic League, and whose bigamy in 1540 disgraced the cause.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is a pastoral counsel bent to suit a prince, and it is ours to own. Philip of Hesse pressed Luther, Melanchthon and Bucer for permission to take a second wife, and they gave it in a written and secret opinion, advising that the thing be concealed. The Lord's word on marriage admits no such dispensation: “they twain shall be one flesh” (Mat 19:5), and the prophet's rebuke to men who dealt treacherously with the wife of their youth stands over the whole transaction, for the Lord “hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth” (Mal 2:14).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a reformer who will not be rebuked has stopped reforming, and the apostolic precedent is public: Paul “withstood him to the face” (Gal 2:11) when Peter was to be blamed. No one did that for Philip until the secret was out and the damage done. The right course was open and was not taken, for “whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy” (Pro 28:13), and the dictionary records the counsel as a sin of the Reformers and not merely an embarrassment of the Reformation.

pos: n. (the Wittelsbach duchy that became the most thorough counter-reformation state in Germany, and whose first Protestant author was a woman)
etymology: Latin Bavaria, from the Baiuvarii, the Germanic people of the Danube plain; German Bayern.
biblical_def: Bavaria is the German land in which the Reformation was defeated earliest and most completely, by a method afterwards copied across Catholic Europe. Its dukes never wavered: Lutheran books were banned in 1522, the first executions followed, the university of Ingolstadt under Johann Eck became the intellectual headquarters of the German opposition to Luther, and from 1549 the Jesuits were installed there and given the schools, Peter Canisius among the first. Bavaria thus pioneered the combination of a committed prince, a controlled university and a teaching order that recovered Austria, Bohemia and much of Poland for Rome. Yet the first lay author to publish in defence of the Reformation in German was a Bavarian: Argula von Grumbach, a noblewoman of the duchy, who in 1523 wrote and printed an open letter challenging the theologians of Ingolstadt to debate with her in German or Latin over their treatment of a student forced to recant, and who was answered with abuse and the loss of her husband's office. The Anabaptists of the Danube, among them Hans Hut, were hunted down. The dictionary enters Bavaria because the counter-reformation's working method was invented here, and because the one voice raised against it in print belonged to a woman the duchy could not answer.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to recant as to retract an opinion; a duchy as the territory of a duke; a disputation as a contest by arguments; and a Jesuit as one of the Society of Jesus.
webster_full: RECANT, v. To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration; to unsay what has been said.
DUCHY, n. The territory or dominions of a duke; a dukedom.
DISPUTATION, n. A contest in words or by arguments; a public exercise in argumentation, as in the schools.
JESUIT, n. One of the society of Jesus, so called, founded by Ignatius Loyola; a crafty person; an intriguer.
INQUISITION, n. A court in some Roman Catholic countries for the examination and punishment of heretics.

corruption_summary: Wittelsbach duchy which banned Lutheran books in 1522 and pioneered the counter-reformation method of prince, university and Jesuit school.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the refusal to argue, which Ingolstadt practised as policy. Argula von Grumbach asked for a disputation in a language she could follow and offered to be judged by Scripture; the faculty replied by calling her a silly woman and procuring her husband's dismissal. A party that holds the schools, the press and the magistrate and will still not meet an objection from the text has conceded the only argument that matters, for the standard it declined is the one Scripture sets: “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty of every believer, lettered or not, to be able to answer: “be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15). Argula could, and the dictionary records that she was a laywoman writing in German when the doctors would only write in Latin. The duchy's weapons were the ordinary ones, office, livelihood and prison, and the Lord's warning puts them in proportion: “fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul” (Mat 10:28).

pos: n. (the region of the free cities and the Hohenzollern margraviates, where Nuremberg carried the Reformation in 1525)
etymology: Latin Franconia, the land of the Franks; German Franken, the northern part of modern Bavaria with Nuremberg at its centre.
biblical_def: Franconia is the patchwork of free cities, margraviates and bishoprics in which the Reformation advanced by town councils rather than by princes. Nuremberg, the greatest of the imperial free cities, held a public disputation in March 1525, abolished the mass, and ordered its churches on evangelical lines under Andreas Osiander and Dominicus Schleupner, becoming the first major city of the empire to do so by its own authority; it printed Luther's works in quantity and gave the movement its best engravers. The margraves of Brandenburg-Ansbach and Brandenburg-Kulmbach carried their territories over, and the Schwabach Articles of 1529, drawn up for the Ansbach and Nuremberg churches, were a step toward the Augsburg Confession. Against this stood the prince-bishops of Wurzburg and Bamberg and the memory of the Peasants' War, which ran through Franconia in 1525 with castles burned and reprisals to match. The Anabaptist Hans Hut gathered congregations through the region before his death in 1527. The dictionary enters Franconia because its Reformation was made by councillors, printers and schoolmasters in self-governing towns, which is a different thing from a prince's decree and tended to last better.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a free city as one governing itself under the empire; a margrave as a German title of nobility; an article as a distinct part of a confession; and a council as a body of men assembled for consultation.
webster_full: FREE CITY, n. A city which governs itself by its own laws, acknowledging only the general sovereignty of the empire.
MARGRAVE, n. A title of nobility in Germany, originally the governor of a march or frontier province.
ARTICLE, n. A single clause or particular in a contract, account or system of doctrine; a distinct proposition.
COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
ENGRAVER, n. One who engraves; a cutter of letters, figures or devices on stone, metal or wood.

Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.

corruption_summary: Region of free cities and Hohenzollern margraviates where Nuremberg abolished the mass by council decree in 1525 and the Schwabach Articles were drawn in 1529.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the Reformation imposed from above and therefore owned by nobody, and Franconia is where the opposite was tried. Nuremberg's council called a public disputation first, heard both sides for a fortnight, and acted afterwards; what followed was a settlement the burghers had sat through and could defend. “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14) is not a democratic slogan but a plain observation, and the apostolic precedent is a gathering: “the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter” (Act 15:6).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that reform proceeds in order and through examined men. The congregation at Jerusalem was told to “look ye out among you seven men of honest report” (Act 6:3), and the rule over the whole business is that “all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). Franconia also carries the warning: the Peasants' War of 1525 burned through the same towns and villages, and a movement which had just learned to act by disputation was blamed for men who acted by fire.

pos: n. (the south-west German region of free cities, where the Peasants' Twelve Articles were drafted and the Tetrapolitan Confession framed)
etymology: Latin Suevia, from the Suebi named by Caesar and Tacitus; German Schwaben, the land between the Black Forest, the Danube and the Alps.
biblical_def: Swabia is the region of imperial free cities in which the Reformation took its most civic form and met its hardest social question. Ulm, Memmingen, Reutlingen, Esslingen, Nordlingen, Lindau, Kempten and Biberach each reformed by their own council and preacher, and Johannes Brenz at Schwabisch Hall became the region's ablest theologian and the author of a catechism used for centuries. At Memmingen in February and March 1525 the peasants of Upper Swabia, meeting with the preacher Christoph Schappeler and the furrier Sebastian Lotzer, drew up the Twelve Articles, the most reasonable document the Peasants' War produced: they asked for the right of each parish to choose and dismiss its minister, the abolition of serfdom, relief from death-taxes and illegal rents, and offered to submit every article to Scripture. Within months the risings were crushed with great slaughter. Swabian cities also framed the Tetrapolitan Confession, presented at Augsburg in 1530 by Strasbourg, Constance, Memmingen and Lindau, a statement standing between Wittenberg and Zurich on the Supper. The dictionary enters Swabia because the Twelve Articles put the hardest question of the Reformation to the Reformers, and because the answer they got was mostly the sword.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines serfdom as the condition of a servile tenant; a tithe as a tenth part; an article as a distinct clause or proposition; and a furrier as a dealer in furs.
webster_full: SERF, n. A servant or slave employed in husbandry, and in some countries attached to the soil, and transferred with it.
TITHE, n. The tenth part of the increase annually arising from the profits of land and stock, allotted to the clergy.
ARTICLE, n. A single clause or particular in a contract or system of doctrine; a distinct proposition.
FURRIER, n. A dealer in furs; one who dresses and prepares furs.
BONDAGE, n. Slavery or involuntary servitude; captivity; imprisonment; restraint of a person's liberty.

Isa 8:20

corruption_summary: South-west German region of free cities where the Twelve Articles of the peasants were drafted at Memmingen in 1525 and the Tetrapolitan Confession framed in 1530.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the withholding of wages and of liberty by men who had just been taught that they were justified freely. The Twelve Articles asked nothing that Scripture does not require of a master, and they offered to be judged by it. The law protects the hired servant: “Thou shalt not oppress an hired servant that is poor and needy” (Deu 24:14), and the apostle says plainly what became of the Swabian rents, that “the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields” (Jam 5:4) cries out against those who kept it back by fraud.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the gospel's liberty has consequences in a man's dealings with his tenants, and that a peasant who asks for them is not thereby a rebel. The jubilee is in the law for a reason: “proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof” (Lev 25:10). The dictionary also holds the peasants to their own offer. They proposed that every article be tried by “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20), and those among them who went on to burn castles abandoned the ground they had chosen.

pos: n. (the north-west German region of the Munster kingdom of 1534 and of the peace of 1648 that ended the wars of religion)
etymology: German Westfalen, the western Falen or plain-dwellers, as against the Ostfalen; Latin Westphalia.
biblical_def: Westphalia carries the Reformation's worst episode and its final settlement, both named after it. In 1534 and 1535 the city of Munster was seized by Melchiorite Anabaptists who proclaimed it the New Jerusalem, expelled all who would not be rebaptised, abolished private property, instituted polygamy, crowned the Dutch tailor Jan van Leiden as king, and held out through a siege that ended in starvation and the public torture of the leaders, whose bodies were hung in cages from the tower of St Lambert's church, where the cages remain. The episode was used for three centuries to discredit every form of believers' baptism, and it is the reason Menno Simons spent his life insisting on nonresistance. More than a century later, in the same region, the Peace of Westphalia was concluded at Munster and Osnabruck in 1648, ending the Thirty Years War, extending the Augsburg settlement to include the Reformed, and fixing the religious map of Germany. Westphalia also held real Reformed life: the academy at Steinfurt, and Philipp Nicolai, who wrote two of the greatest German hymns while burying a thousand of his people in a plague at Unna. The dictionary enters Westphalia because the same region holds the madness and the peace.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fanatic as one wild in religious opinions; polygamy as the having of more wives than one; a treaty as an agreement between nations; and a plague as a pestilence.
webster_full: FANATIC, n. A person affected by excessive and unreasonable zeal, particularly in religious matters; an enthusiast.
POLYGAMY, n. A plurality of wives or husbands at the same time; the having of more than one wife at once.
TREATY, n. An agreement, league or contract between two or more nations or sovereigns, formally signed.
PLAGUE, n. A malignant contagious fever; a pestilence; any thing troublesome or vexatious.
CAGE, n. A box or enclosure made of boards or of wire, for confining birds or beasts.

corruption_summary: North-west German region where Anabaptist fanatics held Munster in 1534 and 1535, and where the Peace of 1648 ended the wars of religion.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the claim of fresh revelation, which produced at Munster every horror attributed to it. Jan Matthys and Jan van Leiden governed by dreams and prophecies, and from those prophecies came the expulsions, the common property, the polygamy and the crown. Scripture provides the test and the men of Munster failed it in public: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jo 4:1), and the prophet's word covers them exactly, that they “speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD” (Jer 23:16).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the testing of teachers by their doctrine and their lives, since “Ye shall know them by their fruits” (Mat 7:16), and the fruit at Munster was visible within a year. The dictionary also refuses the use Munster was put to: that false prophets arise within the church is foretold, for “there shall be false teachers among you” (2Pe 2:1), and their rising does not condemn the doctrine they corrupt. The peace signed in the same region in 1648 was not a triumph of truth but an exhaustion, and it gave the Reformed churches of the empire their legal standing.

pos: n. (the duchy between the Elbe and Denmark where Lutheran preaching began in 1522 and by which it entered the Danish kingdom)
etymology: German Holstein, from Old Saxon Holseta, the dwellers in the wood; held with Schleswig by the Danish crown and the Gottorp dukes.
biblical_def: Holstein is the duchy through which the Reformation entered Scandinavia. German-speaking, lying between the Elbe and the Danish border and bound to the Danish crown, it heard Lutheran preaching very early: Hermann Tast was preaching evangelically at Husum by 1522, reportedly in the churchyard when the church was closed to him, and the towns of Flensburg, Kiel and Itzehoe followed. Duke Christian, who governed Schleswig and Holstein before he became Christian III of Denmark, had been present at the Diet of Worms in 1521 and came away convinced; he established the Reformation in his duchies, and when he won the Danish civil war and the crown in 1536 he brought the same settlement to Denmark and Norway, inviting Johannes Bugenhagen from Wittenberg to draw up the church ordinance and to crown him in 1537. Holstein is therefore the hinge: a German duchy whose prince carried the Lutheran order into two kingdoms, and whose own churches were ordered on Bugenhagen's pattern of a superintendent, a catechising ministry and a school in every town. The dictionary enters Holstein because the Scandinavian Reformation is usually told as a royal act, and the preaching in a Husum churchyard came first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an ordinance as a rule established by authority; a superintendent as one who has the oversight; a churchyard as the ground adjoining a church; and to catechise as to instruct by question and answer.
webster_full: ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; an established rite or ceremony.
SUPERINTENDENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.
CHURCHYARD, n. The ground adjoining a church, in which the dead are buried; a cemetery.
CATECHISE, v. To instruct by asking questions, receiving answers, and offering explanations and corrections.
HINGE, n. The hook or joint on which a door or gate turns; that on which any thing depends or turns.

corruption_summary: Duchy between the Elbe and Denmark where Hermann Tast preached evangelically from 1522, and whose duke carried the Lutheran order into Denmark and Norway in 1536.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the history that begins with the king and forgets the preacher. The Danish and Norwegian Reformations are commonly dated from Christian III's victory in 1536 and Bugenhagen's ordinance of 1537, which is true as far as the law goes; what made the duke a Lutheran was preaching he had heard, and what made Holstein ready was fifteen years of it in towns and churchyards. The command stands on the preacher before it reaches the prince: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2), and a churchyard in Husum is out of season.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the ordinary persistence of house-to-house teaching, which is what Bugenhagen's ordinance then organised across three kingdoms. The apostolic pattern is given twice: Paul taught “publickly, and from house to house” (Act 20:20), and the first disciples “ceased not to teach and preach Jesus Christ” (Act 5:42) daily in the temple and in every house. The commission that sent Tast into the churchyard is the same that sent Bugenhagen to Copenhagen, to “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15).

“preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15) — a duchy's settlement carried into two kingdoms.

pos: n. (the Baltic duchy Lutheran from 1549, whose university at Rostock and whose Chytraeus shaped the Formula of Concord)
etymology: German Mecklenburg, from the castle of Mikilenburg, the great fortress, near Wismar; the land was Slavic Wendish before German settlement.
biblical_def: Mecklenburg is the Baltic duchy whose theologians did the patient work of settling the Lutheran church's internal quarrels. Its towns, Rostock, Wismar and Gustrow, were Hanseatic and took Lutheran preaching in the 1520s and 1530s; the duchy's estates and dukes settled the Reformation formally at the diet of Sternberg in 1549, and a church ordinance followed. The university of Rostock, founded in 1419, became one of the chief Lutheran faculties of the north and taught Scandinavians, Balts and Germans alike. Its greatest figure was David Chytraeus, professor there from 1551 for half a century, who drew up the Mecklenburg church ordinance, reorganised the university at Rostock and others besides, visited and reported on the Lutheran congregations of Austria and Styria, and was one of the six authors of the Formula of Concord of 1577, the document that ended twenty-five years of quarrelling among Luther's heirs over free will, good works, the Supper and adiaphora. Heinrich Plutschau, one of the first two Lutheran missionaries to India in 1706, was a Mecklenburger. The dictionary enters Mecklenburg because the Formula of Concord was mostly committee work done by professors in small northern towns, and it saved the Lutheran churches from dissolving into parties.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines concord as agreement between persons; adiaphora as things indifferent; a formula as a prescribed form of words; and a visitation as the act of visiting for inspection.
webster_full: CONCORD, n. Agreement between persons; union in opinions, sentiments, views or interests; peace; harmony.
INDIFFERENT, a. Neither good nor bad; having no influence or preponderating weight; of a middle nature.
FORMULA, n. A prescribed form; a rule or model; a stated form of words in which anything is expressed.
VISITATION, n. The act of visiting, especially for inspection, or the examination of a church or diocese.
FACULTY, n. The body of professors or masters in a university, or in one of its departments.
scriptures: Eph 4:3
Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
Phi 2:2
Fulfil ye my joy, that ye be likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me.
corruption_summary: Baltic duchy Lutheran from the diet of Sternberg in 1549, whose Rostock professor David Chytraeus helped write the Formula of Concord in 1577.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the party spirit that turns a church's theologians into factions, which is what happened among Luther's heirs after his death in 1546. Philippists against Gnesio-Lutherans, Osiander's doctrine of justification, Major's claim that good works are necessary to salvation, the quarrel over whether ceremonies imposed by an enemy are indifferent: each dispute had a real question in it and each produced pamphlets of extraordinary bitterness. The apostolic charge is the remedy: “that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that unity is laboured for and not assumed, which is what the word rendered endeavouring means: “Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph 4:3). The Formula of Concord took six men years of drafting and visiting and persuading, and the dictionary counts that among the Reformation's real achievements. The end aimed at is the Lord's own petition, “That they all may be one” (Joh 17:21), and the means is that the brethren be “likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind” (Phi 2:2).

pos: n. (the central German land of Erfurt and the Wartburg, where Luther was made a monk and where he translated the New Testament)
etymology: Latin Thuringia, from the Thuringii, a Germanic people subdued by the Franks; German Thüringen.
biblical_def: Thuringia is the land in which Luther was formed and in which the Reformation's worst internal enemy arose. He entered the Augustinian cloister at Erfurt in 1505 and was ordained there, and Erfurt's university gave him his philosophy and his first disgust at it. After the Diet of Worms his prince hid him in the Wartburg above Eisenach from May 1521 to March 1522, and in those ten months he translated the New Testament from Erasmus's Greek into a German that fixed the literary language of the nation; it was printed at Wittenberg in September 1522. In the same years Thomas Muntzer, preaching at Allstedt and then Muhlhausen, moved from reformation to revolution, taught an inward word of the Spirit above the written word, called for the slaughter of the godless, and led the peasants to destruction at Frankenhausen in May 1525, where he was taken and beheaded. Jena's university was founded in 1558 and became the stronghold of the strict Lutheran party. The dictionary enters Thuringia because within four years and forty miles it produced the German New Testament and the first armed claim that the Spirit speaks apart from the Scriptures, and the second is still the Reformation's most persistent counterfeit.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cloister as a monastery; a translation as the act of rendering into another language; revelation as the disclosure of truth by God; and sedition as a tumultuous rising against authority.
webster_full: CLOISTER, n. A monastery or nunnery; a house inhabited by monks or nuns.
TRANSLATION, n. The act of turning into another language; the rendering of something written or spoken into another tongue.
REVELATION, n. The act of disclosing or discovering to others what was before unknown; the direct communication of truth from God to man.
SEDITION, n. A factious commotion of the people; a tumultuous assembly rising in opposition to law.
CASTLE, n. A house fortified for defense against an enemy; a fortress.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
Thus saith the LORD of hosts, Hearken not unto the words of the prophets that prophesy unto you: they make you vain: they speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
corruption_summary: Central German land of Erfurt's cloister and the Wartburg, where Luther translated the New Testament in 1521, and where Muntzer led the peasants to Frankenhausen in 1525.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the inner light set above the written word, and Muntzer is its first armed example. He held that a man who has only the Scriptures has a dead letter, that the living voice of the Spirit speaks in the elect directly, and that this voice had told him to take the sword against the godless. The whole of it is refuted by the standard Scripture gives for testing any voice whatever: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). His end came as the Lord said it would, that “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Mat 26:52).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the written word is more certain than any experience, including a true one. Peter had seen the transfiguration and heard the Father's voice, and he still wrote of it: “We have also a more sure word of prophecy” (2Pe 1:19), to which men do well to take heed. The prophetic word against the Allstedt preaching is plain, that such men “speak a vision of their own heart, and not out of the mouth of the LORD” (Jer 23:16). The Wartburg answered Muntzer before Muntzer spoke: ten months of work on a Greek text, and a nation given the word it could read.

pos: n. (the south German duchy restored to Duke Ulrich in 1534, whose church order under Brenz became the model Lutheran establishment)
etymology: German Württemberg, from the castle of Wirtemberg above Stuttgart; the county became a duchy in 1495.
biblical_def: Wurttemberg is the duchy where the Lutheran church order was worked out most completely and lasted longest. Duke Ulrich, driven from his lands in 1519 by the Swabian League, recovered them by force in 1534 with Hessian help, and introduced the Reformation at once through two men of different schools, Erhard Schnepf for the Lutheran south-east and Ambrosius Blarer for the Zwinglian-leaning west, who agreed a formula on the Supper that let the duchy be reformed as one body. The lasting work was Johannes Brenz's. Brought from Schwabisch Hall, he drafted the catechism, the visitation articles and finally the Great Church Order of 1559, which set up a consistory, a system of parish visitations, a Latin school in every town, and the cloister schools and the Tubingen Stift that took promising boys from the villages, boarded them free, and carried them through to the university. For three centuries Wurttemberg's pastors and schoolmasters came through that pipeline, and so did Kepler, Hegel and Schelling. The dictionary enters Wurttemberg because the Great Church Order is the answer to the question of what a reformed state actually does on the Monday after it reforms, and the answer is schools.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a consistory as an ecclesiastical court; a visitation as the act of visiting for inspection; a stipend as a settled pay; and a seminary as a place of education.
webster_full: CONSISTORY, n. A place of justice in a spiritual court; an assembly of ecclesiastical persons for the regulation of a church.
VISITATION, n. The act of visiting for the purpose of inspection, or the examination of a church, a diocese or a school.
STIPEND, n. Settled pay or compensation for services, whether daily, monthly or annual.
SEMINARY, n. A place of education; any school, academy, college or university in which young persons are instructed.
ORDER, n. Regular disposition; a rule or regulation; a settled mode of proceeding.
scriptures: Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
Eph 6:4
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
corruption_summary: South German duchy reformed from 1534, whose Great Church Order of 1559 under Brenz established consistory, visitations, town schools and the Tubingen Stift.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the reform that is a sermon and no settlement, which Brenz's church order was designed to prevent. A duchy can abolish the mass in a week and be without catechised children in a generation; what Wurttemberg did instead was to write down who examines the minister, who visits the parish, who teaches the boys and who pays for them. The apostolic charge contemplates exactly this handing on: the things heard are to be committed “to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2), which is a description of a seminary.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the household and the school as the ordinary instruments of the church's continuance. Fathers are charged to “bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4), and the promise over early teaching is that “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6). The order itself rests on the apostolic rule that in the church “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40), which in 1559 meant a Latin school in every town and a free place for a village boy with a head on him.

“Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6) — a Latin school in every town of the duchy, 1559.

pos: n. (the Rhineland electorate that became Germany's Reformed power and gave the churches the Heidelberg Catechism in 1563)
etymology: Latin Palatinatus, from comes palatinus, the count of the palace; German Kurpfalz, the electoral Palatinate on the middle Rhine.
biblical_def: The Palatinate is the German electorate that chose the Reformed side and paid the heaviest price for it. Its religion followed its electors with unusual violence: Lutheran under Frederick II and Otto Henry, Reformed under Frederick III from 1559, Lutheran again under Louis VI, Reformed again under John Casimir. Frederick III's settlement is the one that mattered. He had the Heidelberg Catechism drawn up in 1563 by Zacharias Ursinus and Caspar Olevianus with the Heidelberg faculty, a catechism of 129 questions divided into man's misery, his deliverance and his thankfulness, warm in tone and personal in address, which became the most widely loved confessional document of the Reformed churches and is binding in Dutch, German, Hungarian and American Reformed bodies to this day. Heidelberg's university became the Reformed faculty of the empire and sheltered exiles from France, the Netherlands and Italy. Then in 1619 the elector Frederick V accepted the Bohemian crown, lost it at White Mountain in a year, and brought the whole weight of the Thirty Years War onto his own country: the Palatinate was occupied, devastated, stripped of its electoral vote, and in 1622 the Heidelberg library was carted off to Rome. The dictionary enters the Palatinate because the catechism has outlived the electorate by four centuries.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an elector as a prince entitled to vote for the emperor; a catechism as instruction by question and answer; comfort as consolation under affliction; and gratitude as thankfulness for favours received.
webster_full: ELECTOR, n. One who elects; a prince of the German empire who had a voice in the election of the emperor.
CATECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
COMFORT, n. Relief from pain or distress; consolation; support under calamity or affliction.
GRATITUDE, n. An emotion of the heart, excited by a favor received; thankfulness.
MISERY, n. Great unhappiness; extreme pain of body or mind; wretchedness; distress.
scriptures: Rom 14:8
For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's.
What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?
Rom 7:24
O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?
Rom 12:1
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
corruption_summary: Rhineland electorate, Reformed under Frederick III, which produced the Heidelberg Catechism in 1563 and was devastated after 1620 for its elector's Bohemian adventure.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to be named is the prince's ambition charged to the church's account. Frederick V took the Bohemian crown in 1619 against sober advice, held it a winter, and his own country was invaded, burned and occupied for a generation as a result, its library sent to the Vatican and its electoral dignity given to Bavaria. The Palatinate's ministers and people had no part in the decision and bore the whole cost of it, and the dictionary says plainly that this was a dynastic gamble and not a confessional necessity.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the catechism's own: that a Christian's comfort does not depend on his country's fortunes, because he is not his own. “ye are not your own” (1Co 6:19) is the ground of its first question and answer, and the whole of it is summed in the apostle's word that “whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's” (Rom 14:8). The catechism's three parts follow Scripture's own order: the cry “O wretched man that I am!” (Rom 7:24), then the deliverance, then the thankfulness that presents the body “a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God” (Rom 12:1).
